claims.text: The starting material is an HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy in an as-sintered polycrystalline state.
The baseline alloy has a quasi-static yield strength of 786 MPa.
The baseline alloy has a quasi-static compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The baseline alloy has a quasi-static fracture strain of 13.5%.
The proposed intervention is adding approximately 5–10 vol% nanoscale TiC or HfC dispersoids to the HfZrTiTa0.53 matrix.
Mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering will produce a uniform dispersion of the ceramic particles.
Nanoscale TiC or HfC particles will act as barriers to dislocation motion in the alloy matrix.
The ceramic dispersoids will provide sites that promote dynamic grain refinement during high-strain-rate deformation.
Dislocation impediment and dynamic grain refinement will increase work-hardening capacity.
Increased work hardening will delay strain localization and increase uniform deformation before failure.
The dispersoids will absorb and redistribute impact energy, thereby reducing catastrophic energy release.
Relative to the matched baseline, the modified alloy will have 10–20% higher yield and compressive strengths.
Relative to the matched baseline, the modified alloy will have a 20–40% increase in uniform fracture strain.
The modified alloy will exhibit a later onset of strain localization and adiabatic shear banding.
The modified alloy will exhibit lower post-failure temperature spikes and slower crack propagation, interpreted as reduced impact-induced catastrophic energy release.
The predicted effects apply under ambient-temperature adiabatic dynamic compression at strain rates from 10^2 to 10^4 s^-1.
Dispersoid fractions above 10 vol% may embrittle the alloy.
At substantially higher strain rates or elevated temperatures, dispersoid stability and effectiveness may decrease.
